# Sonar Picket Playbook

**HIDING**
When choosing where to hide, avoid the center cells (4-5-6) initially as they are common default choices. Rotate through different zones across rounds rather than staying in one area. After being hit, move away from that cell; after being missed, consider that the shooter may adjust. Track who fired at you and anticipate their next shot will adjust based on their miss pattern. When leading significantly late in the game, move to corner cells (1, 9) or edges (2, 8) to escape predictable center clustering—corners are psychologically less obvious than middle retreats. A corner cell like 1 can work well when you have a substantial lead and need to survive rather than score.

**STATION NOTES**
Use notes sparingly and for genuine coordination, not empty signaling. Early cooperation talk wastes space and doesn't change behavior. Once a note like "steady on station" is established with other boats, maintain it consistently across rounds—consistency itself signals stability and reduces uncertainty. Keep notes minimal and factual. Don't try to manipulate through notes; use them only when you have real tactical information to share. Neutral holding signals like "steady on station" repeated by all boats reinforce mutual non-aggression without being false.

**FIRING**
Fire at your standing order target. Vary your fire cell rather than repeating the same number—this becomes predictable to your target and wastes hits. Don't cluster shots in the center; spread across the board to cover more ground. When you have a lead late in the game, understand your standing order target may adjust their hiding based on your pattern, so vary cells across the full range rather than staying in the middle. In the final rounds, fire at cells your target is likely to retreat to after you've established a pattern—if you've fired center multiple times, they'll likely move to edges or corners, so fire there. Edge cells (2, 8) and corners (1, 9) become viable targets in final rounds when your opponent expects you to follow your earlier pattern.

**CLAIMS**
When the office tells you the true result of your shot, file that result honestly. Do not lie on your claim even in the final round. The office knows the truth and validates it. False claims damage your credibility and may trigger official penalties. Your score matters more than a single round's deception. Honesty builds trust and enables better coordination with other boats. A final round hit should be claimed as a hit.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**
Track which boats might escort you and which you might escort back for mutual 5-point gains. Don't claim escort with boats unless you have actual coordination and can verify it happened. When you don't know if an escort happened, say none rather than guessing. Late in the game when leading, securing mutual escorts is a lower priority than avoiding being hit—focus on survival over incremental gains. Without explicit prior agreement or confirmed mutual hiding/firing pattern, don't claim an escort.

**OVERALL STRATEGY**
Build and maintain a reputation for honesty on shot claims. This matters because deception creates instability and reduces the benefit of any coordination. Protect your lead by hiding unpredictably once you're ahead—move to corners and edges, not just center adjustments. Don't rely on center cells. Vary everything: hide cells, fire cells, and patterns. Acknowledge when a tactic fails and adjust immediately rather than repeating it. When you've established a consistent hiding pattern, enemies will target based on that pattern, so break it in the final rounds by moving to extreme positions they won't predict. Against an opponent who has missed you three times in a row (same area), assume they will adjust their targeting away from that area in their next attempt, making that zone temporarily safer for you.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing a hiding position, vary between central positions (4-6) and edge positions (1-3, 7-9) unpredictably. Track which positions I've used and rotate away from them. If I notice a shooter has hit me twice in a row, move to a position I haven't used in recent rounds rather than trying to predict their next guess. In later rounds, if a shooter has missed me consistently (three or more times), they may be locked into a pattern—edge positions that break from my early central tendencies are worth exploring. Note: I was hit in rounds 3 and 4 from position 5, then in round 5 the shooter missed. Continuing to use position 5 centrally is risky against an active shooter. Move to edges (1-3 or 7-9) when under sustained fire, and track the shooter's miss patterns to identify if they've adjusted.

## Station Notes
Use my notes to signal stability and readiness. Keep notes consistent and bland—avoid sending information that reveals my strategy or position patterns to the table. "Steady on station" is reliable and has proven effective throughout the game. Continue this approach.

## Firing
Always follow the standing order. I will fire at the designated target (in my case, Gamma). For cell selection, use position 5 (center) as a reliable opening, then vary based on observed patterns. Don't overthink cell selection in early rounds; fire positions should be spread to explore the line rather than clustered. If I land a hit early, continue rotating my firing cells to explore different parts of the line rather than staying clustered around a successful position. I hit Gamma in round 1 at position 5 and again in round 2, then missed in rounds 4, 5, and 6 at positions 4, 7, and 5. After landing early hits, I did not return to proven positions or narrow my search pattern effectively. Next time: after a hit, fire at nearby cells in the next round to pursue the target, then rotate if misses continue.

## Claims
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, claim it truthfully every time. The claim must match the private result I receive. There is no value in lying about hits and misses. I maintained this discipline and should continue.

## Escort Coordination
Track which boats might be willing to trade mutual escort claims for the 5-point payoff. When I claim to have escorted another boat, choose one that is likely to claim back. If I have no information about escort patterns, claim none rather than guess randomly. Mutual escort claims (5 points each) are worth more than a single shot (4 points), so establishing this coordination should be a priority for mid-game rounds. In this episode I scored 4 points (one hit) and made no escort claims. I ended with 5 points total but secured nothing from coordination. I must begin speculative escort claims by round 2 or 3 with the boat I judge most likely to reciprocate based on their notes and station behavior. Do not wait for perfect information. A failed mutual claim (4 points lost) is offset by two successful mutual claims (10 points gained). Start earlier and commit to one partner.

## Overall Strategy
The payoff for hitting a target (4 points) is modest. The payoff for mutual escort claims (5 points each) exceeds a single shot. Invest mental effort in identifying which other boat might be willing to coordinate escort claims with me across multiple rounds. Don't waste rounds firing at Harbor—the threat is real and the payoff marginal. Establish escort coordination with one other boat by round 2 or 3, even if speculatively—the 5-point mutual payout compounds quickly and will outpace sporadic hits. In this episode I scored 4 points from one hit against Gamma and 0 from escort claims, finishing at +4 total. Echo finished at +12, suggesting they either landed more hits or captured mutual escort claims I missed. Next game, sacrifice one round of shooting speculation to commit to an escort partner early (likely based on bland, stable notes from other boats). The six-round format is short; coordination must begin immediately, not after establishing certainty.

# Sonar Picket Checker Playbook

## Hiding

When choosing where to hide, avoid predictable patterns. Don't stay in the same cell round after round—rotate your position to make targeting harder. After observing which boats are firing at you consistently, move away from the cells where they've been hitting you. Central positions are reasonable for opening rounds, but vary them rather than anchoring to any single cell.

Track my own hiding history across the game. If I've used a cell recently, move away from it. If an opponent has hit me in a cell, strongly avoid returning there. If an opponent has missed repeatedly in a cell, they may be adapting, so don't assume safety.

I must track not just where I've hidden, but which cells I've already exposed to each firing opponent. Once I hide in a cell and my position becomes known through a hit or through the full round's information, that cell loses some defensive value because that opponent has concrete data about my presence there. Rotate more aggressively away from cells I've already revealed, even if they resulted in misses for my opponent.

## Station Notes

Post "steady on station" consistently. This is cooperative language that costs nothing and helps establish predictability in my own positioning, which I control. Don't overcomplicate my notes. Maintain this through the final round as part of the overall strategy of controlling what I can control.

## Firing

Follow the standing order without deviation. I have no discretion here—fire at my assigned target because that's the rule. Choose my fire cell based on pattern observation of where my target has been hiding recently. If I've hit a target before in a cell, they're likely to move away from it; if I've missed repeatedly in a cell, they may not be there. Look for recent rotation patterns in their hiding, not just individual cell history.

Against a target with strong recent behavior (like a hit in a previous round), assume they will rotate to a neighboring or nearby alternative cell rather than moving randomly. This narrows the search space more effectively than scattering shots across the full line.

After hitting a target, do not assume they will use the same defensive avoidance pattern in the next round that they used after I hit them before. Targets may adapt their adaptation. Watch for second-order patterns: if a target moved from cell 5 to cell 6 after I hit them in round 5, they may not move to cell 6 again in round 6 if they anticipate I'll follow them there. Look for variation in their evasion behavior itself.

## Claims

Always file claims that match the private result the office gives me. This is mandatory and non-negotiable for game integrity. False claims corrupt my own decision-making in future rounds because I lose track of what's actually happening, and I cannot extract strategic value from a lie that only I know about. The office knows the truth; other players learn my patterns through observation. Lying to myself serves no one.

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I match my claim to that result exactly. No exceptions, no matter what strategic intuition suggests.

## Escort Claims

When I name an escort, I need mutual recognition for the 5-point payoff. Name none unless I have a clear pre-established signal with another boat or have already observed mutual escort-naming in previous rounds. Don't guess. The penalty for an unreciprocated escort claim is silence—no points either way—so the risk-reward is asymmetric. Only name an escort when I have evidence of prior mutual intent.

During this game, I saw no mutual escort signals emerge among other boats either. Maintain the assumption that escort claims require either an explicit prior coordination (which I haven't established with anyone) or observed evidence of mutual naming from earlier rounds. Until I see such evidence, name none.

## Overall Strategy

Pay close attention to which boats are targeting me and where they're hitting. Adjust my hiding accordingly. Observe which boats' hit and miss patterns indicate skill versus luck or random firing. Prioritize defensive positioning over all other considerations since I take 1 point per hit.

Track the standing order strictly and fire mechanically at my assigned target while varying fire cells based on observed opponent movement. Cooperate through consistent notes but compete through evasion and accurate shooting. The game rewards both reliable positioning information and hard-target defense; balance attention between understanding what others are doing and making myself hard to find.

In the final rounds, maintain all prior strategies—don't break discipline in round 6 just because points are running out. Consistency of approach compounds over time.

My final score was -2. I fired 6 times and achieved 1 hit (4 points), filed claims accurately throughout, and was hit multiple times by other boats. My hiding strategy was not aggressive enough in rotation. I need to move further and faster away from cells I've already exposed, and I need to recognize that after being hit, my opponent now has concrete information about one of my positions and will likely hunt nearby cells in the next firing opportunity. This is not just about varying position; it's about treating a hit as a strong signal that the cell I used and its neighbors are now high-probability targets in the next round.
